CHAPTER 9 - NUTRITION IN PLANTS: MINERAL NUTRITION

Introduction

Living organisms need a continuous supply of nutrients to build their bodies, grow, repair worn-out parts and release energy. Plants are remarkable because most of them can manufacture their own food from very simple raw materials - carbon dioxide, water and minerals - using the energy of sunlight. This chapter deals with mineral nutrition: the mineral elements plants absorb (mainly from the soil), why these elements are essential, the different roles they play, the symptoms that appear when they are deficient, how scientists find out which elements a plant needs, how minerals are actually taken up by roots, and the special modes of nutrition adopted by insectivorous, symbiotic, parasitic and saprophytic plants.

9.1 MODES OF NUTRITION

Nutrition is the process by which an organism obtains and utilises food. On the basis of how they obtain their food, organisms are grouped as autotrophs and heterotrophs.

AUTOTROPHIC NUTRITION: Autotrophs (auto = self, trophos = nourishing) prepare their own organic food from inorganic raw materials. Green plants are photoautotrophs - they use light energy in photosynthesis to convert carbon dioxide and water into carbohydrates, releasing oxygen. Some bacteria are chemoautotrophs; they obtain energy by oxidising inorganic substances such as ammonia, nitrites or hydrogen sulphide instead of using light. All green plants are essentially autotrophic for carbon, but they still depend on the soil for their mineral supply.

HETEROTROPHIC NUTRITION: Heterotrophs (hetero = other) cannot make their own food and depend, directly or indirectly, on autotrophs. Animals, fungi, most bacteria and a few flowering plants are heterotrophic. Among plants, heterotrophic nutrition appears in special forms - parasitic plants that draw food from a host, saprophytic plants that feed on dead organic matter, and insectivorous plants that supplement their nitrogen supply by trapping insects. Thus although the majority of plants are autotrophic, several interesting exceptions exist.

9.2 ESSENTIAL MINERAL ELEMENTS AND THE CRITERIA OF ESSENTIALITY

Plants take in a large number of elements from the soil, but not all of them are necessary for growth. Some are absorbed simply because they are present in the soil solution. To decide which elements are truly required, plant physiologists (notably Arnon and Stout, 1939) laid down definite CRITERIA OF ESSENTIALITY. An element is regarded as ESSENTIAL if it satisfies the following conditions:

(a) The element must be absolutely necessary for normal growth and reproduction. In its absence the plant cannot complete its life cycle.

(b) The requirement must be SPECIFIC and not replaceable by another element. For example, the role of magnesium cannot be taken over by any other element.

(c) The element must be DIRECTLY involved in the metabolism of the plant - as a part of an essential metabolite (for example nitrogen in proteins, magnesium in chlorophyll) or as an activator of enzymes.

On the basis of these criteria, seventeen elements are today regarded as essential for most higher plants. Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen are obtained from carbon dioxide and water; the remaining elements are absorbed as mineral ions from the soil.

9.3 MACRONUTRIENTS AND MICRONUTRIENTS

Essential elements are divided into two groups according to the QUANTITY in which the plant needs them.

MACRONUTRIENTS (major elements) are required in relatively LARGE amounts (generally more than 1 to 10 millimoles per kilogram of dry matter, or above about 0.1 per cent of the dry weight). The nine macronutrients are carbon (C), hydrogen (H), oxygen (O), nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), potassium (K), calcium (Ca), magnesium (Mg) and sulphur (S). Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen come from air and water; the other six are absorbed from the soil.

MICRONUTRIENTS (minor elements or trace elements) are required in very SMALL amounts (generally less than 0.1 per cent of the dry weight, often only a few parts per million). Even though the quantity is tiny, they are just as essential as the macronutrients. The eight micronutrients usually listed are iron (Fe), manganese (Mn), zinc (Zn), copper (Cu), boron (B), molybdenum (Mo), chlorine (Cl) and nickel (Ni). A deficiency of a micronutrient is as harmful as a deficiency of a macronutrient, and an excess can be toxic.

9.4 ROLE (FUNCTIONS) OF THE MAJOR ELEMENTS

Each essential element has definite functions. The main roles of the macronutrients are as follows.

NITROGEN (N): Absorbed mainly as nitrate (NO3-) and ammonium (NH4+). Nitrogen is a constituent of proteins, nucleic acids (DNA and RNA), amino acids, chlorophyll, ATP and many enzymes and vitamins. It is required by the plant in the greatest amount among the soil-derived elements and strongly promotes vegetative (leafy) growth.

PHOSPHORUS (P): Absorbed as phosphate ions (H2PO4- and HPO4^2-). Phosphorus is a component of cell membranes (phospholipids), nucleic acids, ATP and other energy-carrying molecules, and of many phosphorylated intermediates. It is essential for energy transfer, root development, flowering and fruiting.

POTASSIUM (K): Absorbed as the potassium ion (K+). It is the most abundant cation in the cell. Potassium maintains the ionic balance and turgor of cells, activates many enzymes, is involved in protein synthesis, and controls the opening and closing of stomata through the guard cells. It is required in large amounts by growing tissues.

CALCIUM (Ca): Absorbed as the calcium ion (Ca2+). Calcium is a constituent of the middle lamella (as calcium pectate) that holds cells together, is needed during cell division and in the formation of the cell wall and mitotic spindle, regulates membrane permeability and acts as a second messenger and enzyme activator.

MAGNESIUM (Mg): Absorbed as the magnesium ion (Mg2+). Magnesium is the central atom of the chlorophyll molecule, so it is indispensable for photosynthesis. It also activates the enzymes of respiration and photosynthesis (including those of carbon fixation) and takes part in the synthesis of DNA and RNA and in ribosome structure.

SULPHUR (S): Absorbed as the sulphate ion (SO4^2-). Sulphur is present in the amino acids cysteine and methionine, and hence in many proteins. It is also a part of coenzyme A, several vitamins (thiamine, biotin) and ferredoxin.

Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen form the framework of all organic molecules - carbohydrates, proteins, fats and nucleic acids - and are obtained from carbon dioxide and water rather than from the soil.

9.5 ROLE (FUNCTIONS) OF THE MICRONUTRIENTS

IRON (Fe): Required for the synthesis of chlorophyll (though it is not a part of it), and is a constituent of cytochromes and ferredoxin, the electron carriers of respiration and photosynthesis. Iron is absorbed as ferric (Fe3+) or ferrous (Fe2+) ions and is needed in the largest amount among the micronutrients.

MANGANESE (Mn): Activates many enzymes of respiration, photosynthesis and nitrogen metabolism. Its best-known role is in the splitting of water (photolysis) during the light reaction of photosynthesis, which releases oxygen.

ZINC (Zn): Activates several enzymes, especially carboxylases, and is needed for the synthesis of the plant hormone auxin (indole acetic acid) and of tryptophan.

COPPER (Cu): An essential part of certain redox enzymes (for example plastocyanin and cytochrome oxidase) and is involved in the electron-transport reactions of photosynthesis and respiration.

BORON (B): Required for the uptake and utilisation of calcium, for pollen germination, cell elongation, cell differentiation and the translocation of sugars and carbohydrates. Boron does not activate enzymes but is essential all the same.

MOLYBDENUM (Mo): A component of the enzymes nitrogenase and nitrate reductase, and hence essential for nitrogen fixation and nitrate assimilation. It is needed in the smallest amount of all the essential elements.

CHLORINE (Cl): As the chloride ion (Cl-) it helps, along with sodium and potassium, in maintaining the solute concentration and the anion-cation balance of the cell, and is essential (with manganese) for the water-splitting reaction that evolves oxygen in photosynthesis.

NICKEL (Ni): A constituent of the enzyme urease and needed for the metabolism of urea; it is also required by nitrogen-fixing bacteria. It was the most recently recognised essential micronutrient.

9.6 MINERAL DEFICIENCY SYMPTOMS

When an essential element is not available in sufficient quantity, the plant shows characteristic DEFICIENCY SYMPTOMS. The symptoms depend on two things: the function of the element and whether the element can be moved (is mobile) within the plant. Mobile elements (such as nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium and magnesium) are withdrawn from the older leaves and moved to the young growing regions, so their deficiency symptoms appear FIRST in the OLDER leaves. Immobile elements (such as calcium, sulphur, iron and boron) cannot be re-exported, so their deficiency symptoms appear FIRST in the YOUNGER leaves.

The common visible symptoms are:

CHLOROSIS - the loss of chlorophyll leading to YELLOWING of the leaves. It is caused by the deficiency of nitrogen, potassium, magnesium, sulphur, iron, manganese, zinc or molybdenum. Nitrogen and magnesium deficiency yellows the older leaves first; iron deficiency yellows the younger leaves first.

NECROSIS - the DEATH of tissue, usually of the leaf, appearing as dead brown spots or patches. It is caused by the deficiency of calcium, potassium or magnesium.

STUNTED GROWTH - poor or retarded growth of the plant, with short internodes and a general reduction in size, caused especially by a lack of nitrogen, phosphorus or sulphur.

Other symptoms include the inhibition of cell division, delayed or no flowering, premature fall of leaves and buds, and the accumulation of anthocyanin producing purplish or reddish leaves (typical of phosphorus deficiency). Because more than one element can produce the same symptom (for instance chlorosis), the pattern of symptoms - which leaves are affected and in what way - is used to identify the deficient element.

9.7 METHODS OF STUDYING THE MINERAL REQUIREMENTS OF PLANTS

To find out which elements are essential and what each does, plants are grown in a medium of KNOWN and CONTROLLED composition, from which any one element can be left out. Two classic techniques are used.

HYDROPONICS (WATER CULTURE): The plant is grown with its roots dipped not in soil but in a water solution containing all the mineral nutrients in known amounts (a defined nutrient solution). Julius von Sachs (1860) first grew plants to maturity in such a solution. To test whether a particular element is essential, it is simply omitted from the solution (this is called the deficiency or omission experiment) and the plant is watched for deficiency symptoms. The solution must be aerated so that the roots get oxygen. Hydroponics is now also used commercially to grow vegetables and flowers without soil.

SAND (or GRAVEL) CULTURE: Here the plants are grown in purified sand or gravel that is chemically inert and provides only support; the required nutrients are supplied by watering the sand with a nutrient solution of known composition. Sand culture gives the roots better anchorage and aeration than water culture.

In both methods, growing a plant in a complete nutrient solution and comparing it with plants from which one element at a time has been withheld allows the essential elements and the effect of each deficiency to be established.

9.8 MECHANISM OF ABSORPTION OF MINERALS

Minerals are present in the soil as ions dissolved in the soil water. Because the concentration of most ions is usually LOWER in the soil solution than inside the root cells, and because ions are electrically charged and cannot cross the membrane freely, their uptake needs special mechanisms. The absorption of minerals is generally described as taking place in two phases.

PASSIVE ABSORPTION (or passive uptake): In the first, rapid phase, ions move INTO the free space of the root (the cell walls and intercellular spaces, called the apparent free space) by simple DIFFUSION, down their concentration gradient, WITHOUT the use of metabolic energy. This phase does not require respiration and can occur even in dead tissue. Ion exchange and mass flow of the soil solution also help.

ACTIVE ABSORPTION (or active uptake): In the second, slower phase, ions are moved ACROSS the cell membrane into the cytoplasm, often AGAINST their concentration gradient. This needs metabolic ENERGY supplied by respiration in the form of ATP, and it is carried out by specific CARRIER PROTEINS (ion carriers or pumps) embedded in the membrane. Because active uptake needs energy, it is reduced by low temperature, by lack of oxygen and by respiratory poisons. The involvement of carriers explains why the uptake of a particular ion is SELECTIVE and shows saturation - the rate levels off when all the carriers are occupied.

Once inside the root cells, ions move from cell to cell and are finally loaded into the xylem, through which, along with water, they are carried up to the leaves and other parts of the plant.

CRITICAL CONCENTRATION AND TOXICITY: For each element there is a CRITICAL CONCENTRATION - the minimum tissue concentration below which growth is reduced and deficiency symptoms appear. Below this level the plant suffers deficiency. On the other hand, when an element is present in EXCESS it may become TOXIC. Any mineral ion, when its concentration in the tissue rises high enough to reduce the dry weight of the tissue by about ten per cent, is said to have reached its toxic level. Micronutrients, needed in tiny amounts, cross into the toxic range more easily than macronutrients. The toxicity of one element can also show up as the deficiency of another - for example an excess of manganese can induce a deficiency of iron, magnesium and calcium.

9.9 SPECIAL MODES OF NUTRITION IN PLANTS

Although most plants are autotrophic, some have evolved special ways of obtaining nutrients, particularly nitrogen, from unusual sources.

INSECTIVOROUS (CARNIVOROUS) PLANTS: These green plants photosynthesise normally but grow in nitrogen-poor, marshy or acidic soils. To make up for the shortage of nitrogen, they trap and digest small insects. Their leaves are modified into traps. In the pitcher plant (Nepenthes) the leaf forms a pitcher with a lid; insects that fall in are digested by enzymes in the fluid. In the sundew (Drosera) the leaf bears sticky, gland-tipped hairs (tentacles) that hold and digest the insect. In the Venus flytrap (Dionaea) the leaf is a hinged trap that snaps shut. In the bladderwort (Utricularia), an aquatic plant, tiny bladders suck in small water animals. Digestion of the trapped animal supplies the plant with nitrogen and other minerals.

SYMBIOTIC NUTRITION: Here two organisms of different kinds live together for mutual benefit. The classic example is the association between leguminous plants (such as pea, gram and beans) and the bacterium Rhizobium. The bacterium lives in swellings called ROOT NODULES on the roots of the legume; it FIXES atmospheric nitrogen into compounds the plant can use, while the plant supplies the bacterium with food and shelter. Another example is MYCORRHIZA, a partnership between a fungus and the roots of higher plants (for example pine): the fungal threads greatly increase the surface for the absorption of water and minerals (especially phosphorus) and pass them to the plant, while the plant gives the fungus sugars.

PARASITIC NUTRITION: A parasitic plant obtains its food from another living plant, the host, to which it does harm. A total (complete) parasite such as the dodder (Cuscuta) is a leafless, non-green twining plant that sends sucking roots called HAUSTORIA into the host's tissues and draws both water and food from it. A partial parasite such as the mistletoe (Loranthus, Viscum) is green and can photosynthesise but taps the host's xylem for water and minerals. Some parasites (like Rafflesia) grow on the roots of the host.

SAPROPHYTIC NUTRITION: Saprophytes obtain their nourishment from DEAD and decaying organic matter, which they digest outside the body by secreting enzymes and then absorb. Most fungi (such as mushrooms, Mucor and yeast) and some bacteria are saprophytes; a few non-green flowering plants (such as Monotropa, the Indian pipe) are also saprophytic. Saprophytes are important as decomposers that recycle nutrients in nature.

9.10 ROLE OF NUTRIENTS IN METABOLISM - AN OVERVIEW

Taken together, the essential elements build the plant body and run its chemistry. Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen form the backbone of every organic molecule. Nitrogen, sulphur and phosphorus are built into proteins, nucleic acids and energy carriers. Magnesium and nitrogen are needed for chlorophyll and hence for photosynthesis; iron, copper, manganese and chlorine drive the electron-transport and water-splitting reactions of respiration and photosynthesis. Potassium, calcium and chlorine maintain ionic balance, turgor and membrane function. Many micronutrients (manganese, zinc, copper, molybdenum, nickel) act as activators or components of enzymes, so that a tiny quantity controls large amounts of chemistry. A balanced supply of all the essential elements, neither too little (deficiency) nor too much (toxicity), is therefore necessary for healthy growth, and this understanding is the basis of the use of fertilisers in agriculture.

SUMMARY

- Nutrition is the intake and use of food. Autotrophs (green plants, some bacteria) make their own food; heterotrophs (animals, fungi and a few plants) depend on others. Special heterotrophic modes in plants are insectivorous, symbiotic, parasitic and saprophytic nutrition.
- An element is essential (criteria of Arnon and Stout) if it is absolutely necessary for growth and reproduction, its role is specific and not replaceable, and it is directly involved in metabolism. Seventeen elements are essential for higher plants.
- Macronutrients (needed in large amounts): C, H, O, N, P, K, Ca, Mg, S. Micronutrients or trace elements (needed in tiny amounts): Fe, Mn, Zn, Cu, B, Mo, Cl, Ni.
- Major roles: N - proteins, nucleic acids, chlorophyll; P - ATP, membranes, nucleic acids; K - turgor, stomata, enzyme activation; Ca - middle lamella, cell wall, membranes; Mg - central atom of chlorophyll; S - amino acids cysteine and methionine. Micronutrients act mostly as enzyme activators or parts of electron carriers (Fe, Cu), the water-splitting system (Mn, Cl), nitrogen metabolism (Mo, Ni) and auxin synthesis (Zn).
- Deficiency symptoms: chlorosis (yellowing from loss of chlorophyll), necrosis (death of tissue) and stunted growth. Mobile-element deficiencies (N, P, K, Mg) show first in older leaves; immobile-element deficiencies (Ca, S, Fe, B) show first in younger leaves.
- Mineral requirements are studied by growing plants in defined media - hydroponics (water culture, Sachs) and sand culture - and omitting one element at a time (deficiency experiments).
- Absorption of minerals occurs in two phases: passive absorption (diffusion into the free space, no energy) and active absorption (across the membrane against the gradient, needing ATP and carrier proteins). Below the critical concentration a plant is deficient; in excess an element becomes toxic.
- Special nutrition: insectivorous plants (Nepenthes, Drosera, Dionaea, Utricularia) trap insects for nitrogen; symbiotic legume-Rhizobium fixes nitrogen and mycorrhiza aids phosphorus uptake; parasites (Cuscuta) draw food through haustoria; saprophytes (many fungi, Monotropa) feed on dead matter.
- A balanced supply of all essential elements, avoiding both deficiency and toxicity, is essential for healthy plant growth and is the scientific basis of fertiliser use.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Nutrition in Plants: Mineral Nutrition (NIOS Senior Secondary Biology)
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Answer short-answer questions in 2-4 sentences and long-answer questions in detail with examples where asked. Marks are shown against each question.

questions.question: State the criteria of essentiality used to decide whether a mineral element is essential for a plant.
questions.answer: According to Arnon and Stout, an element is essential if: (1) it is absolutely necessary for the normal growth and reproduction of the plant, so that in its absence the plant cannot complete its life cycle; (2) its requirement is specific and cannot be replaced by any other element; and (3) it is directly involved in the metabolism of the plant, either as a part of an essential metabolite or as an activator of enzymes.
questions.explanation: The three Arnon-Stout criteria.

questions.question: Name the nine macronutrients and state the ion in which nitrogen and phosphorus are absorbed.
questions.answer: The nine macronutrients are carbon (C), hydrogen (H), oxygen (O), nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), potassium (K), calcium (Ca), magnesium (Mg) and sulphur (S). Nitrogen is absorbed mainly as nitrate (NO3-) and ammonium (NH4+) ions, and phosphorus is absorbed as phosphate ions (H2PO4- and HPO4 2-).
questions.explanation: List of macronutrients plus the ionic forms of N and P.

questions.question: Why is magnesium considered indispensable for photosynthesis?
questions.answer: Magnesium is the central atom of the chlorophyll molecule, and chlorophyll is the pigment that traps light energy in photosynthesis. Without magnesium chlorophyll cannot be formed, so photosynthesis cannot take place. Magnesium also activates several enzymes of photosynthesis and respiration, including those of carbon fixation.
questions.explanation: Mg is the central atom of chlorophyll and an enzyme activator.

questions.question: Distinguish between macronutrients and micronutrients, giving two examples of each.
questions.answer: Macronutrients are essential elements required by plants in relatively large amounts (above about 0.1 per cent of dry weight), for example nitrogen and potassium. Micronutrients (trace elements) are required in very small amounts (only a few parts per million), for example iron and zinc. Although micronutrients are needed in tiny quantities, they are just as essential as macronutrients, and an excess of them easily becomes toxic.
questions.explanation: Difference is the quantity required; both are essential.

questions.question: What is chlorosis? Name any two elements whose deficiency causes it.
questions.answer: Chlorosis is the yellowing of leaves caused by the loss or reduced formation of chlorophyll. It is a common deficiency symptom. It is caused by a deficiency of nitrogen or magnesium (yellowing older leaves first) and of iron (yellowing younger leaves first); potassium, sulphur, manganese, zinc and molybdenum deficiencies can also cause chlorosis.
questions.explanation: Chlorosis = yellowing from chlorophyll loss; N, Mg, Fe etc.

questions.question: Why do the deficiency symptoms of nitrogen appear first in the older leaves, while those of calcium appear first in the younger leaves?
questions.answer: Nitrogen is a mobile element - it can be withdrawn from the older leaves and moved to the actively growing young leaves when it is in short supply. So the older leaves lose nitrogen first and show symptoms first. Calcium is an immobile element - once fixed it cannot be re-exported to the young tissues, so when calcium is scarce the young growing leaves are starved first and show symptoms first.
questions.explanation: Mobility of the element decides which leaves are affected first.

questions.question: Describe the two classic methods used to study the mineral requirements of plants, and explain how a deficiency experiment shows that an element is essential.
questions.answer:
To study mineral requirements, plants are grown in a medium of known and controlled composition so that any element can be added or left out at will.

(1) Hydroponics (water culture): the plant is grown with its roots in a defined nutrient solution containing all the minerals in known amounts, instead of in soil. Julius von Sachs first grew plants to maturity this way. The solution is aerated so the roots get oxygen.

(2) Sand (or gravel) culture: plants are grown in purified, chemically inert sand that gives only support and anchorage, and the required nutrients are supplied by watering the sand with a nutrient solution of known composition.

Deficiency (omission) experiment: to test whether a particular element is essential, that one element is omitted from an otherwise complete nutrient solution while another set of plants is grown in the complete solution. If the plants lacking the element show abnormal growth or characteristic deficiency symptoms and cannot complete their life cycle, whereas the control plants grow normally, the omitted element is proved to be essential and its specific role can be worked out.
questions.explanation: Hydroponics and sand culture; omission of one element proves essentiality.

questions.question: Explain the mechanism of mineral absorption by roots under the headings passive absorption and active absorption. How do critical concentration and toxicity relate to mineral supply?
questions.answer:
Minerals are present in the soil as charged ions dissolved in soil water, usually at a lower concentration than inside the root cells, so their uptake needs special mechanisms and is described in two phases.

Passive absorption: In the first, rapid phase, ions enter the free space of the root (cell walls and intercellular spaces) by simple diffusion down their concentration gradient, without using metabolic energy. It does not need respiration and can occur even in dead tissue; ion exchange and mass flow assist it.

Active absorption: In the second, slower phase, ions are carried across the cell membrane into the cytoplasm, often against their concentration gradient. This needs metabolic energy (ATP from respiration) and specific carrier proteins (ion pumps) in the membrane. Because it needs energy it is slowed by low temperature, lack of oxygen and respiratory poisons, and because it uses carriers it is selective and shows saturation.

Critical concentration is the minimum tissue concentration of an element below which growth is reduced and deficiency symptoms appear; below it the plant is deficient. When an element is present in excess it becomes toxic (roughly when it lowers the tissue dry weight by about 10 per cent). Micronutrients turn toxic more easily because they are needed in tiny amounts, and toxicity of one element can induce the deficiency of another.
questions.explanation: Passive (diffusion, no energy) vs active (ATP, carriers, against gradient); critical concentration and toxicity.

questions.question: How do insectivorous plants obtain nitrogen? Give two examples with the trap involved.
questions.answer: Insectivorous (carnivorous) plants are green and photosynthesise, but they grow in nitrogen-poor marshy or acidic soils, so they trap and digest small insects to obtain nitrogen. Their leaves are modified into traps. Examples: in the pitcher plant (Nepenthes) the leaf forms a pitcher with a lid and digests insects that fall into its fluid; in the sundew (Drosera) the leaf has sticky gland-tipped hairs that hold and digest the insect. (Utricularia, the bladderwort, sucks small animals into tiny bladders.)
questions.explanation: They trap insects for nitrogen; Nepenthes (pitcher), Drosera (sticky hairs).

questions.question: Compare symbiotic, parasitic and saprophytic modes of nutrition in plants with suitable examples.
questions.answer:
Symbiotic nutrition: two organisms of different kinds live together for mutual benefit. In the legume-Rhizobium association the bacterium lives in root nodules of legumes (pea, gram) and fixes atmospheric nitrogen for the plant, while the plant supplies food and shelter. In mycorrhiza a fungus lives on plant roots and helps absorb water and minerals (especially phosphorus) in return for sugars.

Parasitic nutrition: a parasite draws food from a living host, harming it. A total parasite such as the dodder (Cuscuta) is leafless and non-green and sends sucking roots (haustoria) into the host to take both water and food; a partial parasite such as the mistletoe (Loranthus) is green but taps the host's xylem for water and minerals.

Saprophytic nutrition: saprophytes obtain nourishment from dead and decaying organic matter, which they digest externally by secreting enzymes and then absorb. Most fungi (mushrooms, Mucor) and some non-green flowering plants (Monotropa) are saprophytes and act as decomposers, recycling nutrients.

Thus symbionts benefit each other, parasites harm a living host, and saprophytes feed on dead matter.
questions.explanation: Symbiosis (mutual benefit, Rhizobium/mycorrhiza), parasite (Cuscuta, harms host), saprophyte (Monotropa, dead matter).

questions.question: Differentiate between autotrophic and heterotrophic nutrition.
questions.answer: Autotrophic nutrition is the mode in which an organism prepares its own organic food from inorganic raw materials, for example green plants using light in photosynthesis. Heterotrophic nutrition is the mode in which an organism cannot make its own food and depends, directly or indirectly, on autotrophs, for example animals and fungi.
questions.explanation: Autotrophs make food; heterotrophs depend on others.

questions.question: What is meant by an essential element? Name the two broad groups into which essential elements are divided.
questions.answer: An essential element is a mineral element that is absolutely necessary for the normal growth and reproduction of a plant, whose role is specific and cannot be replaced by another element, and which is directly involved in metabolism. Essential elements are divided into macronutrients (needed in large amounts) and micronutrients or trace elements (needed in very small amounts).
questions.explanation: Essential = necessary, specific, involved in metabolism; macro and micro.

questions.question: Explain the three criteria of essentiality with one example each.
questions.answer: (1) The element must be absolutely necessary for growth and reproduction - e.g. without nitrogen a plant cannot complete its life cycle. (2) Its requirement must be specific and non-replaceable - e.g. the role of magnesium cannot be taken over by any other element. (3) It must be directly involved in metabolism, as part of a metabolite or as an enzyme activator - e.g. nitrogen in proteins or magnesium in chlorophyll.
questions.explanation: Necessity, specificity, direct metabolic involvement, with examples.

questions.question: State any two functions of potassium in plants.
questions.answer: Potassium maintains the ionic balance and turgor of cells and activates many enzymes. It is also involved in protein synthesis and controls the opening and closing of stomata through the guard cells.
questions.explanation: K: turgor/ionic balance, enzyme activation, stomata.

questions.question: Describe the roles of nitrogen and phosphorus in the plant.
questions.answer: Nitrogen is a constituent of proteins, nucleic acids (DNA and RNA), amino acids, chlorophyll, ATP and many enzymes and vitamins; it is needed in the largest amount among soil elements and promotes vegetative growth. Phosphorus is a component of cell membranes (phospholipids), nucleic acids and ATP and other energy-carrying molecules; it is essential for energy transfer, root development, flowering and fruiting.
questions.explanation: N: proteins, nucleic acids, chlorophyll; P: ATP, membranes, nucleic acids.

questions.question: State two functions of calcium in plants.
questions.answer: Calcium is a constituent of the middle lamella (as calcium pectate) that holds adjacent cells together, and it is needed during cell division and in the formation of the cell wall and mitotic spindle. It also regulates membrane permeability and acts as an enzyme activator and second messenger.
questions.explanation: Ca: middle lamella, cell division/wall, membrane function.

questions.question: In which ionic forms are sulphur and potassium absorbed, and give one function of sulphur.
questions.answer: Sulphur is absorbed as the sulphate ion (SO4 2-) and potassium as the potassium ion (K+). Sulphur is present in the amino acids cysteine and methionine and hence in many proteins; it is also a part of coenzyme A and some vitamins.
questions.explanation: S as SO4 2-, K as K+; S is in cysteine/methionine.

questions.question: Name any four micronutrients and state the role of manganese.
questions.answer: Four micronutrients are iron (Fe), manganese (Mn), zinc (Zn) and copper (Cu). Manganese activates many enzymes of respiration, photosynthesis and nitrogen metabolism, and it is especially involved in the splitting of water (photolysis) during the light reaction of photosynthesis, which releases oxygen.
questions.explanation: Fe, Mn, Zn, Cu; Mn activates enzymes and splits water.

questions.question: Why is molybdenum important despite being needed in the smallest amount?
questions.answer: Molybdenum is a component of the enzymes nitrogenase and nitrate reductase. Nitrogenase is needed for the fixation of atmospheric nitrogen and nitrate reductase for the assimilation of nitrate. So although molybdenum is required in the smallest amount of all the essential elements, it is indispensable for nitrogen metabolism.
questions.explanation: Mo is in nitrogenase and nitrate reductase - key for N metabolism.

questions.question: State the roles of iron and copper in the plant.
questions.answer: Iron is required for the synthesis of chlorophyll (although it is not a part of it) and is a constituent of the cytochromes and ferredoxin, the electron carriers of respiration and photosynthesis. Copper is an essential part of certain redox enzymes such as plastocyanin and cytochrome oxidase and takes part in the electron-transport reactions of photosynthesis and respiration.
questions.explanation: Fe: chlorophyll synthesis, cytochromes; Cu: redox enzymes.

questions.question: Give one function each of zinc, boron and chlorine.
questions.answer: Zinc activates several enzymes and is needed for the synthesis of the hormone auxin (indole acetic acid). Boron is required for pollen germination, cell elongation and the translocation of sugars, and for the utilisation of calcium. Chlorine (as chloride) helps maintain the anion-cation balance of the cell and, with manganese, is needed for the water-splitting reaction of photosynthesis.
questions.explanation: Zn: auxin; B: pollen/sugar translocation; Cl: ionic balance/water split.

questions.question: Define chlorosis and necrosis.
questions.answer: Chlorosis is the loss of chlorophyll leading to yellowing of the leaves, caused by the deficiency of elements such as nitrogen, magnesium or iron. Necrosis is the death of plant tissue, usually of the leaf, appearing as dead brown spots or patches, caused by the deficiency of calcium, potassium or magnesium.
questions.explanation: Chlorosis = yellowing; necrosis = tissue death.

questions.question: A plant shows yellowing that begins in the older leaves. A second plant shows yellowing that begins in the younger leaves. What does each pattern indicate?
questions.answer: Yellowing (chlorosis) beginning in the older leaves indicates a deficiency of a MOBILE element, such as nitrogen or magnesium, which is withdrawn from old leaves and sent to the young growing leaves. Yellowing beginning in the younger leaves indicates a deficiency of an IMMOBILE element, such as iron, which cannot be re-exported from the old leaves to the young tissue. Thus the position of the symptom reveals whether the deficient element is mobile or immobile.
questions.explanation: Old-leaf chlorosis = mobile (N, Mg); young-leaf chlorosis = immobile (Fe).

questions.question: Why is the pattern of deficiency symptoms, rather than a single symptom, used to identify the deficient element?
questions.answer: Because more than one element can produce the same visible symptom - for example chlorosis can result from a lack of nitrogen, magnesium, iron, sulphur and others. Therefore a single symptom is not enough; the whole pattern (which leaves are affected, whether old or young, and the exact nature of the symptom) must be studied to identify the particular deficient element.
questions.explanation: Symptoms overlap, so the full pattern is diagnostic.

questions.question: What is hydroponics? State one commercial use of it.
questions.answer: Hydroponics (water culture) is the technique of growing plants with their roots dipped in a nutrient solution of known composition instead of in soil, the solution being aerated so the roots get oxygen. Commercially it is used to grow vegetables and flowers without soil.
questions.explanation: Hydroponics = soil-less water culture; used for commercial crops.

questions.question: How is a deficiency (omission) experiment carried out and what does it reveal?
questions.answer: In a deficiency experiment a plant is grown in a complete nutrient solution while a similar plant is grown in a solution from which one element has been omitted. The plants are watched for growth and symptoms. If the plant lacking the element shows deficiency symptoms and grows abnormally compared with the control, it reveals that the omitted element is essential and shows what its deficiency does.
questions.explanation: Omit one element; abnormal growth reveals essentiality and the role.

questions.question: Distinguish between passive and active absorption of minerals.
questions.answer: Passive absorption is the rapid entry of ions into the free space (cell walls and intercellular spaces) of the root by simple diffusion down their concentration gradient; it needs no metabolic energy and can occur even in dead tissue. Active absorption is the slower movement of ions across the cell membrane into the cytoplasm, often against the concentration gradient; it needs metabolic energy (ATP) and specific carrier proteins, and is reduced by low temperature and lack of oxygen.
questions.explanation: Passive: diffusion, no energy; active: against gradient, ATP + carriers.

questions.question: What is meant by critical concentration and toxic level of an element?
questions.answer: The critical concentration is the minimum concentration of an element in the tissue below which growth is reduced and deficiency symptoms appear. The toxic level is the concentration at which an element, present in excess, damages the plant - conventionally when it reduces the tissue dry weight by about ten per cent. Below the critical concentration the plant is deficient; above the toxic level it is poisoned.
questions.explanation: Critical = deficiency threshold; toxic = excess damaging threshold.

questions.question: Why is active absorption of minerals reduced when the soil becomes waterlogged or the temperature falls?
questions.answer: Active absorption needs energy from respiration (ATP) and working carrier proteins. Waterlogging drives oxygen out of the soil, so root respiration falls and less ATP is available; a fall in temperature also slows respiration and enzyme activity. With less energy the carrier proteins cannot pump ions against the gradient, so active uptake of minerals is reduced.
questions.explanation: Both cut respiration/ATP, so carrier-driven active uptake slows.

questions.question: Why are insectivorous plants said to trap insects, yet are still green?
questions.answer: Insectivorous plants grow in nitrogen-poor marshy or acidic soils, so they trap and digest insects to obtain the nitrogen (and some minerals) that the soil cannot supply. They remain green and carry out photosynthesis normally for their carbon and energy needs; the insects only supplement their nitrogen supply.
questions.explanation: They photosynthesise for food but trap insects for nitrogen.

questions.question: Describe the mutual benefits in the legume-Rhizobium symbiosis and in mycorrhiza.
questions.answer: In the legume-Rhizobium association the bacterium Rhizobium lives in root nodules of legumes and fixes atmospheric nitrogen into compounds the plant can use, while the plant supplies the bacterium with food and shelter. In mycorrhiza a fungus lives in partnership with the roots of a higher plant; the fungal threads greatly increase the surface for absorbing water and minerals (especially phosphorus) and pass them to the plant, while the plant gives the fungus sugars. Both are examples of mutually beneficial symbiosis.
questions.explanation: Rhizobium fixes N for food/shelter; mycorrhiza aids P uptake for sugars.

questions.question: Differentiate between a total parasite and a partial parasite with one example each.
questions.answer: A total (complete) parasite is non-green and cannot photosynthesise, so it draws both water and food from the host through sucking roots called haustoria - for example the dodder (Cuscuta). A partial parasite is green and can photosynthesise its own food but taps the host's xylem for water and minerals - for example the mistletoe (Loranthus).
questions.explanation: Total (Cuscuta): water + food; partial (mistletoe): only water/minerals.

questions.question: Explain the modes of nutrition in living organisms and state where plants fit in each mode.
questions.answer:
Nutrition is the process by which an organism obtains and uses food. On the basis of how food is obtained, organisms are grouped as autotrophs and heterotrophs.

Autotrophic nutrition: autotrophs make their own organic food from inorganic raw materials. Green plants are photoautotrophs - they use light energy in photosynthesis to convert carbon dioxide and water into carbohydrates, releasing oxygen. Some bacteria are chemoautotrophs and obtain energy by oxidising inorganic substances such as ammonia or hydrogen sulphide instead of using light. Most plants are autotrophic for carbon but still take minerals from the soil.

Heterotrophic nutrition: heterotrophs cannot make their own food and depend directly or indirectly on autotrophs. Animals, fungi and most bacteria are heterotrophic. Among plants, heterotrophic nutrition appears in special forms - parasitic plants that draw food from a host (Cuscuta), saprophytic plants that feed on dead organic matter (Monotropa), and insectivorous plants that trap insects to obtain nitrogen (Nepenthes, Drosera). Thus although the majority of plants are autotrophic, several exceptions show heterotrophic modes.
questions.explanation: Autotrophs (photo/chemo) vs heterotrophs; special plant heterotrophy.

questions.question: Give an account of the macronutrients required by plants and the specific role of each of N, P, K, Ca, Mg and S.
questions.answer:
Macronutrients are essential elements needed in relatively large amounts. They are carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium and sulphur. Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen come from carbon dioxide and water; the other six are absorbed from the soil as ions.

Nitrogen (as NO3- and NH4+): a constituent of proteins, nucleic acids, amino acids, chlorophyll, ATP and many enzymes; needed most among soil elements and promotes vegetative growth.
Phosphorus (as phosphate): a component of phospholipid membranes, nucleic acids and ATP; essential for energy transfer, root growth, flowering and fruiting.
Potassium (as K+): maintains turgor and ionic balance, activates enzymes, takes part in protein synthesis and controls stomatal movement.
Calcium (as Ca2+): a constituent of the middle lamella (calcium pectate), needed in cell division and cell-wall and spindle formation, and regulates membrane permeability.
Magnesium (as Mg2+): the central atom of chlorophyll, so vital for photosynthesis, and an activator of respiratory and photosynthetic enzymes.
Sulphur (as SO4 2-): present in the amino acids cysteine and methionine, in coenzyme A and in some vitamins and ferredoxin.
questions.explanation: The nine macronutrients and the specific functions of N, P, K, Ca, Mg, S.

questions.question: Describe the micronutrients required by plants and the role of each.
questions.answer:
Micronutrients (trace elements) are essential elements needed in very small amounts (less than about 0.1 per cent of dry weight), yet they are as essential as the macronutrients. The eight usually listed are iron, manganese, zinc, copper, boron, molybdenum, chlorine and nickel.

Iron (Fe): needed for chlorophyll synthesis and is a part of cytochromes and ferredoxin, the electron carriers; required in the largest amount among micronutrients.
Manganese (Mn): activates enzymes of respiration, photosynthesis and nitrogen metabolism and helps split water in photosynthesis.
Zinc (Zn): activates carboxylases and is needed for the synthesis of auxin.
Copper (Cu): a part of redox enzymes such as plastocyanin and cytochrome oxidase, in electron transport.
Boron (B): needed for calcium uptake and utilisation, pollen germination, cell elongation and sugar translocation.
Molybdenum (Mo): a component of nitrogenase and nitrate reductase, essential for nitrogen fixation and nitrate assimilation; needed in the smallest amount.
Chlorine (Cl): as chloride maintains the anion-cation balance and, with manganese, helps split water in photosynthesis.
Nickel (Ni): a constituent of urease, needed for urea metabolism.
questions.explanation: The eight micronutrients and their individual roles.

questions.question: What are mineral deficiency symptoms? Describe chlorosis, necrosis and stunted growth, and explain how the mobility of an element decides where the symptom first appears.
questions.answer:
When an essential element is not available in sufficient quantity the plant shows characteristic deficiency symptoms, because the metabolic process that depends on the element is disturbed.

Chlorosis is the loss of chlorophyll leading to yellowing of the leaves; it results from a deficiency of nitrogen, magnesium, iron, sulphur, potassium, manganese, zinc or molybdenum. Necrosis is the death of tissue, seen as dead brown spots or patches, caused mainly by a deficiency of calcium, potassium or magnesium. Stunted (retarded) growth, with short internodes and reduced size, follows a shortage of nitrogen, phosphorus or sulphur. Other signs include delayed flowering, premature fall of leaves and buds, and purplish leaves from anthocyanin (phosphorus deficiency).

The site where a symptom first appears depends on whether the element is mobile. Mobile elements (nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, magnesium) can be withdrawn from the older leaves and moved to the young growing regions, so their deficiency shows first in the OLDER leaves. Immobile elements (calcium, sulphur, iron, boron) cannot be re-exported, so their deficiency shows first in the YOUNGER leaves. Because several elements can cause the same symptom, the pattern of symptoms is used to identify the deficient element.
questions.explanation: Chlorosis/necrosis/stunting; mobile -> old leaves, immobile -> young leaves.

questions.question: Describe how the mineral requirements of plants are studied using hydroponics and sand culture.
questions.answer:
To find out which elements a plant needs and what each does, plants are grown in a medium of known and controlled composition so that any element can be added or withheld. Two classic techniques are used.

Hydroponics (water culture): the plant is grown with its roots dipped not in soil but in a defined nutrient solution containing all the mineral nutrients in known amounts. Julius von Sachs first grew plants to maturity in such a solution. The solution must be aerated so the roots get oxygen for respiration. To test whether a particular element is essential it is omitted from the solution (a deficiency or omission experiment) and the plant is watched for symptoms. Hydroponics is now also used commercially to grow vegetables and flowers without soil.

Sand (or gravel) culture: the plants are grown in purified, chemically inert sand or gravel that provides only support and anchorage; the required nutrients are supplied by watering the sand with a nutrient solution of known composition. Sand culture gives better anchorage and aeration than water culture.

In both methods, a plant grown in a complete solution (the control) is compared with plants from which one element at a time is withheld. Abnormal growth and deficiency symptoms in the deprived plants establish which elements are essential and the effect of each deficiency.
questions.explanation: Hydroponics (Sachs) and sand culture; omission experiments with a control.

questions.question: Explain the mechanism of mineral absorption by roots, distinguishing the passive and active phases, and discuss the ideas of critical concentration and toxicity.
questions.answer:
Minerals occur in the soil as charged ions dissolved in soil water, usually at a lower concentration than inside the root cells and unable to cross the membrane freely; so their uptake needs special mechanisms, described in two phases.

Passive absorption: in the first, rapid phase, ions move into the free space of the root (the cell walls and intercellular spaces, the 'apparent free space') by simple diffusion down their concentration gradient, without using metabolic energy. It does not need respiration and can occur even in dead tissue; ion exchange and mass flow of the soil solution assist it.

Active absorption: in the second, slower phase, ions are moved across the cell membrane into the cytoplasm, often against their concentration gradient. This needs metabolic energy (ATP from respiration) and specific carrier proteins (ion pumps) in the membrane. Because it needs energy, active uptake is reduced by low temperature, lack of oxygen and respiratory poisons; because it uses carriers, it is selective and shows saturation. Once inside, ions pass from cell to cell and are loaded into the xylem, which carries them with water to the leaves.

For each element there is a critical concentration - the minimum tissue level below which growth is reduced and deficiency appears. In excess an element becomes toxic (roughly when it lowers dry weight by about 10 per cent). Micronutrients, needed in tiny amounts, turn toxic easily, and the toxicity of one element can show up as the deficiency of another.
questions.explanation: Passive (diffusion) and active (ATP, carriers) uptake; critical concentration and toxicity.

questions.question: Describe insectivorous plants and symbiotic nutrition as special modes of nutrition, with examples.
questions.answer:
Although most plants are autotrophic, some have evolved special ways of obtaining nutrients, especially nitrogen.

Insectivorous (carnivorous) plants: these green plants photosynthesise normally but grow in nitrogen-poor, marshy or acidic soils, so they trap and digest small insects to obtain nitrogen. Their leaves are modified into traps. In the pitcher plant (Nepenthes) the leaf forms a pitcher with a lid and digests insects that fall into its fluid; in the sundew (Drosera) the leaf bears sticky, gland-tipped hairs that hold and digest the insect; in the Venus flytrap (Dionaea) the hinged leaf snaps shut; and in the aquatic bladderwort (Utricularia) tiny bladders suck in small water animals.

Symbiotic nutrition: here two different organisms live together for mutual benefit. In the legume-Rhizobium association the bacterium lives in root nodules of legumes such as pea and gram and fixes atmospheric nitrogen for the plant, while the plant gives it food and shelter. In mycorrhiza a fungus partners the roots of higher plants such as pine; the fungal threads increase the absorbing surface for water and minerals, especially phosphorus, which they pass to the plant, while the plant supplies the fungus with sugars. Both partnerships help the plant obtain nutrients it could not easily get alone.
questions.explanation: Insectivorous plants (Nepenthes, Drosera, Utricularia) and symbiosis (Rhizobium, mycorrhiza).

questions.question: Describe parasitic and saprophytic modes of nutrition in plants with examples, and state their significance.
questions.answer:
Parasitic nutrition: a parasitic plant obtains its food from another living plant, the host, which it harms. A total (complete) parasite such as the dodder (Cuscuta) is a leafless, non-green twining plant that sends sucking roots called haustoria into the host's tissues and draws both water and food from it. A partial parasite such as the mistletoe (Loranthus, Viscum) is green and can photosynthesise its own food but taps the host's xylem for water and minerals. Parasites weaken or damage their hosts and are important pests of crops and trees.

Saprophytic nutrition: saprophytes obtain their nourishment from dead and decaying organic matter, which they digest outside the body by secreting enzymes and then absorb the soluble products. Most fungi (mushrooms, Mucor, yeast) and some bacteria are saprophytes, and a few non-green flowering plants such as Monotropa (the Indian pipe) are also saprophytic.

Significance: saprophytes are the chief decomposers of nature; by breaking down dead bodies and litter they recycle carbon, nitrogen and minerals back into the soil, keeping ecosystems fertile. Parasites, though harmful to their hosts, are part of natural food relationships and population control.
questions.explanation: Parasite (Cuscuta, mistletoe) draws from host; saprophyte (Monotropa, fungi) recycles dead matter.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Elements absorbed by a plant are many, but only some are essential. Arnon and Stout laid down criteria of essentiality: the element must be absolutely necessary for growth and reproduction, its role must be specific and non-replaceable, and it must be directly involved in metabolism. On this basis about seventeen elements are essential for higher plants.
(a) Who proposed the criteria of essentiality?
(b) State any two of the criteria.
(c) From where do plants obtain carbon, hydrogen and oxygen?
(d) Why are all elements found in a plant not called essential?
questions.answer:
(a) The criteria were proposed by Arnon and Stout (1939).
(b) Any two: the element is absolutely necessary for normal growth and reproduction; its requirement is specific and cannot be replaced by another element; it is directly involved in the plant's metabolism.
(c) Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen are obtained from carbon dioxide and water, not from the soil.
(d) Because a plant absorbs many elements simply because they are present in the soil solution; only those that satisfy the criteria (necessary, specific and metabolically involved) are called essential.
questions.explanation: Arnon and Stout; criteria; C, H, O from CO2/water; mere presence is not essentiality.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Macronutrients are needed in large amounts and each has a specific role. Nitrogen builds proteins and chlorophyll, phosphorus is in ATP and membranes, potassium controls stomata and turgor, calcium cements cells in the middle lamella, magnesium lies at the centre of chlorophyll and sulphur is in certain amino acids.
(a) Which element is the central atom of chlorophyll?
(b) Name the element that controls the opening and closing of stomata.
(c) In which two amino acids is sulphur present?
(d) State one role of phosphorus.
questions.answer:
(a) Magnesium is the central atom of the chlorophyll molecule.
(b) Potassium controls the opening and closing of stomata (through the guard cells).
(c) Sulphur is present in the amino acids cysteine and methionine.
(d) Phosphorus is a component of ATP, nucleic acids and phospholipid membranes and is essential for energy transfer, root growth and flowering (any one).
questions.explanation: Mg centre of chlorophyll; K controls stomata; S in cysteine/methionine; P in ATP.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Micronutrients are required in tiny amounts but are indispensable. Iron helps make chlorophyll and forms cytochromes, manganese splits water in photosynthesis, molybdenum is in nitrogenase and nitrate reductase, and zinc is needed for auxin synthesis.
(a) Which micronutrient is required in the largest amount?
(b) Which micronutrient is needed in the smallest amount?
(c) Which micronutrient helps in the splitting of water in photosynthesis?
(d) Which plant hormone needs zinc for its synthesis?
questions.answer:
(a) Iron (Fe) is required in the largest amount among the micronutrients.
(b) Molybdenum (Mo) is needed in the smallest amount.
(c) Manganese (Mn), with chloride, helps in the splitting of water (photolysis) in photosynthesis.
(d) Zinc is needed for the synthesis of the hormone auxin (indole acetic acid).
questions.explanation: Fe largest, Mo smallest; Mn splits water; Zn for auxin.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Deficiency symptoms depend on the function of the element and on whether it is mobile in the plant. Mobile elements (N, P, K, Mg) are moved from old leaves to young ones, so their symptoms appear first in older leaves; immobile elements (Ca, S, Fe, B) show symptoms first in younger leaves. Common symptoms are chlorosis, necrosis and stunted growth.
(a) Define chlorosis.
(b) A plant shows yellowing of the older leaves first. Name the type of element (mobile or immobile) that is deficient and give one example.
(c) Name a symptom that means death of tissue.
(d) Why can the same symptom be caused by more than one element?
questions.answer:
(a) Chlorosis is the loss of chlorophyll leading to yellowing of the leaves.
(b) A mobile element is deficient, because mobile elements are withdrawn from old leaves first; example - nitrogen (or magnesium, potassium).
(c) Necrosis is the death of tissue, seen as dead brown spots.
(d) Because several elements take part in chlorophyll formation and related processes, a deficiency of any of them (for example N, Mg, Fe, S) can disturb chlorophyll and produce the same symptom, chlorosis; so the full pattern must be studied to identify the exact element.
questions.explanation: Chlorosis defined; old-leaf yellowing = mobile (N); necrosis = tissue death; overlapping causes.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
To study which elements are essential, plants are grown in media of known composition. In hydroponics the roots are dipped in an aerated nutrient solution; in sand culture inert sand supplies only support and the nutrients are given as solution. Omitting one element at a time (deficiency experiment) reveals its role.
(a) What is hydroponics?
(b) What is the function of the sand in sand culture?
(c) Why must the nutrient solution be aerated?
(d) How does omitting an element show that it is essential?
questions.answer:
(a) Hydroponics (water culture) is growing plants with their roots in a defined nutrient solution instead of soil.
(b) In sand culture the inert purified sand only gives support and anchorage to the roots; the nutrients are supplied separately as solution.
(c) The solution is aerated so that the roots receive oxygen for respiration, which they need for active absorption of ions.
(d) If a plant grown without a particular element shows deficiency symptoms and abnormal growth compared with a control grown in the complete solution, the omitted element is proved to be essential.
questions.explanation: Hydroponics; sand for support; aeration for O2; omission proves essentiality.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Mineral ions are absorbed in two phases. In passive absorption ions diffuse into the free space of the root without energy. In active absorption ions are pumped across the membrane against the gradient using ATP and carrier proteins. Below the critical concentration the plant is deficient; in excess an element becomes toxic.
(a) Which phase of absorption does not need metabolic energy?
(b) What are the two requirements of active absorption?
(c) Define critical concentration.
(d) Why does a lack of oxygen in the soil reduce mineral uptake?
questions.answer:
(a) Passive absorption does not need metabolic energy; ions simply diffuse into the free space.
(b) Active absorption requires metabolic energy (ATP from respiration) and specific carrier proteins in the membrane.
(c) The critical concentration is the minimum tissue concentration of an element below which growth is reduced and deficiency symptoms appear.
(d) A lack of oxygen slows root respiration, so less ATP is produced; without energy the carrier proteins cannot pump ions against the gradient, and active absorption falls.
questions.explanation: Passive = no energy; active needs ATP + carriers; critical concentration; O2 needed for ATP.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Some green plants growing in nitrogen-poor soils trap insects to obtain nitrogen, using leaves modified into traps such as pitchers, sticky hairs and bladders. Other plants form partnerships: Rhizobium in legume root nodules fixes nitrogen, and mycorrhizal fungi help roots absorb phosphorus.
(a) Why do insectivorous plants trap insects?
(b) Name the trap in Nepenthes and in Drosera.
(c) Where does Rhizobium live and what does it do?
(d) How does a mycorrhiza benefit the plant?
questions.answer:
(a) They grow in nitrogen-poor soils and trap insects to obtain nitrogen (and some minerals) that the soil cannot supply, while still photosynthesising for their food.
(b) In Nepenthes (pitcher plant) the leaf forms a pitcher; in Drosera (sundew) the leaf has sticky gland-tipped hairs (tentacles).
(c) Rhizobium lives in root nodules on the roots of legumes and fixes atmospheric nitrogen into a form the plant can use, receiving food and shelter in return.
(d) The mycorrhizal fungus increases the absorbing surface of the roots and helps take up water and minerals, especially phosphorus, giving them to the plant in exchange for sugars.
questions.explanation: Insects for N; pitcher/sticky hairs; Rhizobium fixes N in nodules; mycorrhiza aids P.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Parasites draw food from a living host. Cuscuta is a leafless non-green total parasite that uses haustoria to take water and food; mistletoe is a green partial parasite that taps the host's xylem. Saprophytes such as Monotropa and many fungi feed on dead organic matter and act as decomposers.
(a) What are haustoria?
(b) Distinguish a total parasite from a partial parasite.
(c) Name a saprophytic flowering plant.
(d) State one ecological role of saprophytes.
questions.answer:
(a) Haustoria are the sucking roots of a parasitic plant that penetrate the host's tissues to draw water and food.
(b) A total parasite (e.g. Cuscuta) is non-green and takes both water and food from the host; a partial parasite (e.g. mistletoe) is green and photosynthesises its own food but taps the host only for water and minerals.
(c) Monotropa (the Indian pipe) is a non-green saprophytic flowering plant.
(d) Saprophytes act as decomposers, breaking down dead organic matter and recycling nutrients back into the soil, which keeps ecosystems fertile.
questions.explanation: Haustoria; total vs partial parasite; Monotropa; decomposers recycle nutrients.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A farmer notices that his wheat crop is pale green with poor leafy growth, while a neighbouring plot given plenty of a certain fertiliser is dark green and leafy. Nitrogen is the soil element needed in the greatest amount and strongly promotes vegetative growth; it is a part of proteins and chlorophyll.
(a) Which element is most likely deficient in the pale crop?
(b) Give two roles of this element in the plant.
(c) In which ionic forms is it absorbed?
(d) Suggest how the farmer can correct the deficiency.
questions.answer:
(a) Nitrogen is most likely deficient, since the crop is pale (chlorotic) with poor leafy growth.
(b) Nitrogen is a constituent of proteins, nucleic acids and chlorophyll and promotes vegetative (leafy) growth; it is also part of ATP and many enzymes (any two).
(c) Nitrogen is absorbed mainly as nitrate (NO3-) and ammonium (NH4+) ions.
(d) The farmer can apply a nitrogen-rich fertiliser (such as urea or ammonium/nitrate fertiliser) or grow a leguminous crop with Rhizobium to restore soil nitrogen.
questions.explanation: Pale + poor growth = N deficiency; roles; NO3-/NH4+; add N fertiliser.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Two potted plants show chlorosis. In plant A the yellowing starts in the oldest leaves; in plant B it starts in the youngest leaves. Mobile elements move out of old leaves to young ones, whereas immobile elements stay put.
(a) In which plant is a mobile element deficient?
(b) Name a mobile element that could be missing in that plant.
(c) Name an immobile element whose deficiency yellows young leaves.
(d) Why does the location of the symptom help diagnose the deficiency?
questions.answer:
(a) In plant A, where the symptom starts in the oldest leaves, a mobile element is deficient.
(b) A mobile element that could be missing is nitrogen (or magnesium or potassium).
(c) Iron is an immobile element whose deficiency causes chlorosis in the young leaves first.
(d) Because a mobile element is withdrawn from old leaves and an immobile one cannot be, the position of the yellowing (old versus young leaves) tells us whether the deficient element is mobile or immobile and so narrows down which element it is.
questions.explanation: A = mobile (N); Fe immobile in young leaves; site reveals mobility.
